Shore
shore
n. (the land bordering the sea; the strand; rendering Hebrew choph and saphah, Greek aigialos)
From the Saxon score, probably from sceran, to shear or cut — the line where the land is cut off by the water. Hebrew saphah is a lip or edge, so the sea shore is literally the sea's lip.

Biblical Definition

The shore is where land meets sea, and Scripture uses it for two things: the sand that measures a promise, and the standing-place of Christ. God's oath to Abraham after Moriah fixes the first: “in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore” (Genesis 22:17). Hebrews takes up the same measure and adds the wonder of it — that from one man, “and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable” (Hebrews 11:12). The shore is the standing image of a number no one can count, given to a childless man. In the Gospels the shore is where the Lord stands to teach and to meet his own. Pressed by crowds, “he went into a ship, and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore” (Matthew 13:2), and from that boat came the parables of the kingdom. And after the resurrection: “when the morning was now come, Jesus stood on the shore: but the disciples knew not that it was Jesus” (John 21:4). They had gone back to fishing and caught nothing; he was already on the beach with a fire of coals and bread, waiting for men who did not recognise him. The shore is where the risen Christ meets returning failures with breakfast.

Webster 1828 Definition

Where land meets sea — in Hebrew, the sea's lip. Its sand measures the promise given a childless man; and it is where Christ sat to teach the parables, and stood at daybreak to feed disciples who had gone back to their nets.

expand to see more

SHORE, n. [Sax. score, from sceran, to shear or cut off.] The coast or land adjacent to the ocean or sea, or to a large lake or river.

2. This word is applied primarily to the land contiguous to water; but it is used for the ground within the flux and reflux of the tide.

3. SHORE, n. A prop; a buttress; something that supports a building.

4. SHORE, v.t. To support by a post or buttress; to prop.

5. In Scripture, the sand which is upon the sea shore, an emblem of number innumerable, Gen. 22.

Key Scripture

Genesis 22:17 — "That in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore; and thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies;"

Hebrews 11:12 — "Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable."

Matthew 13:2 — "And great multitudes were gathered together unto him, so that he went into a ship, and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore."

John 21:4 — "But when the morning was now come, Jesus stood on the shore: but the disciples knew not that it was Jesus."

Modern Corruption

The Abrahamic promise is spiritualised until it means nothing in particular, or narrowed to a single ethnic line — when Paul makes the seed Christ and the heirs all who are of faith.

expand to see more

Two errors handle this promise badly. The first empties it, treating the sand and stars as poetry with no definite fulfilment, so that God's oath after Moriah becomes a warm sentiment. The second narrows it to physical descent alone, which is the assumption behind the dispensational scheme that keeps Israel and the church on permanently separate tracks — a framework unknown to any Reformation confession. Paul settles the sense of the promise in Galatians: the seed is Christ, and if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise (Galatians 3:16, 29). The innumerable multitude of Revelation 7, out of every nation and kindred and people and tongue, is the sand of the sea shore counted.

The principle to recover is the shore of John 21. The disciples had returned to their old trade, fished all night, and taken nothing — and the risen Lord was standing on the beach in the half-light with a fire already lit. He does not begin with rebuke; he asks whether they have any meat, tells them where to cast, and feeds them. The restoration of Peter follows breakfast rather than preceding it. Christians who have gone back to something they left, and are ashamed of the night's catch, should know who is usually standing on the shore at daybreak.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew choph is a coast or haven; saphah is a lip, and so the shore of the sea. Greek aigialos is a beach or strand.

expand to see more

Hebrew choph (H2348) — a coast, shore, haven; Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea.

Hebrew saphah (H8193) — a lip, an edge; the sea shore, literally the sea's lip.

Hebrew chol (H2344) — sand; the measure of the promised seed in Genesis 22:17.

Greek aigialos (G123) — a beach, strand, shore; where the multitude stood and where Christ stood.

Greek ammos (G285) — sand; as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable, Hebrews 11:12.

Usage

"Of the promise measured by sand: as the sand which is upon the sea shore (Genesis 22:17)."

"Of the Lord teaching from a boat: the whole multitude stood on the shore (Matthew 13:2)."

"Of the risen Christ waiting at daybreak: Jesus stood on the shore: but the disciples knew not that it was Jesus (John 21:4)."
